performers: Fyodor Chaliapin, bass; orchestra conducted by Percy Pitt
intro: In Rimsky-Korsakov’s The Prophet, a setting of Pushkin’s poem, a man crossing the desert meets a six-winged angel who tears him apart and remakes him as a prophet. Chaliapin sings with Percy Pitt and orchestra, recorded at Hayes in 1921.

sections.label: A · Andante, the bass voice enters
sections.mNote: The voice opens Pushkin’s vision in measured phrases.

sections.label: B · Voice above rippling accompaniment
sections.mNote: The bass sings of the newly opened senses.

sections.label: C · Orchestral interlude
sections.mNote: The accompaniment links the verses of the poem.

sections.label: D · Bass line moving forward
sections.mNote: The vocal line moves in repeated notes.

sections.label: F · The prophet’s final charge
sections.mNote: Con forza e maestoso (forcefully and majestically).

cues.title: Opening and entry of the bass
cues.text: Firm chords open the song, marked Andante, before the bass voice enters quietly. His first phrases are measured, close to speech. When the six-winged angel appears in Pushkin’s desert, the accompaniment changes to flowing figures beneath the voice.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, Complete Collected Works, vol. 45 (Muzgiz, 1946; reprinted 1970), The Prophet, p. 91: Andante, quiet vocal entry and flowing accompaniment at the appearance of the seraph. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/79/IMSLP20759-PMLP48251-Rimsky_Op49.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Stasov, 1897
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov wrote The Prophet in 1897 and dedicated it to Vladimir Stasov. It is the second of two Pushkin songs published as Op. 49; the first is The Upas Tree.
cues.evidence: Complete Collected Works, vol. 45, p. 91 gives the dedication. The date and titles are catalogued at https://imslp.org/wiki/2_Romances,_Op.49_(Rimsky-Korsakov,_Nikolay).

cues.title: Pushkin’s poem, 1826
cues.text: In Pushkin’s poem the angel opens the man’s eyes and ears, replaces his tongue with a serpent’s sting and puts a burning coal where his heart was. The man lies in the desert like a corpse.
cues.evidence: Pushkin, The Prophet (1826), complete Russian text: https://rvb.ru/pt/pushkin/0420-ru.html. This note describes the poem as a whole.

cues.title: Final invocation, con forza e maestoso
cues.text: The ending is marked con forza e maestoso, “forcefully and majestically”. Chaliapin’s bass sings God’s command. In Pushkin’s 1826 poem the prophet must cross seas and lands and “burn people’s hearts with the word”.
cues.evidence: Complete Collected Works, vol. 45, p. 97, gives the marking and final invocation. The quotation is our translation of Pushkin’s last line: https://rvb.ru/pt/pushkin/0420-ru.html. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/79/IMSLP20759-PMLP48251-Rimsky_Op49.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: Russian composer known for fairy-tale operas and his detailed knowledge of the orchestra; he became a professor before he had learned counterpoint.
facts: Naval College, Saint Petersburg; composition with Balakirev and years of private study
Conservatory professor from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Fifteen operas, from The Maid of Pskov to The Golden Cockerel
composer.background:
Before he had seen the sea, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov rigged a toy brig and read letters from his older brother Voyin, a naval officer. Growing up in Tikhvin, he wanted a ship of his own. His father took him to the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, and his piano lessons continued alongside his naval education. In 1861 his teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Mily Balakirev, who encouraged the seventeen-year-old cadet to begin a symphony.

The clipper Almaz carried him away in 1862 on a voyage of nearly three years. During a long stop in England he wrote the symphony’s slow movement without a piano, and took a chance to try it at a restaurant. He posted the music to Balakirev, who replied with encouragement and requests for changes. Farther out, he saw the Gulf Stream turn the ocean blue, flying fish and phosphorescence. After his return to Russia he took up music again, and Balakirev conducted the completed First Symphony in December 1865.
